title: Find Indices With Index and Value Difference II
statement:
You get a 0-indexed integer array `nums` of length `n` and two integers, `indexDifference` and `valueDifference`. Look for two indices `i` and `j` in `[0, n - 1]` (they are allowed to be the same index) whose positions are at least `indexDifference` apart, `abs(i - j) >= indexDifference`, and whose values are at least `valueDifference` apart, `abs(nums[i] - nums[j]) >= valueDifference`.

Return `[i, j]` for such a pair; when several pairs work, any one of them is accepted. If no pair works, return `[-1, -1]`.
signature: int[] findIndices(int[] nums, int indexDifference, int valueDifference)
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every pair is O(n²), too slow for 10^5 elements. Because the conditions use absolute values, we may assume `i <= j`, so for a fixed `j` the candidates are all `i <= j - indexDifference`, a prefix of the array. Among them, the best partner for `nums[j]` is either the smallest or the largest value in that prefix: if neither is far enough from `nums[j]`, nothing in between is. So keep a running (prefix) minimum and maximum as the prefix grows by one index per step.

## Approach

1. Let `minIndex` and `maxIndex` point at the smallest and largest values of the allowed prefix; both start at 0.
2. Move `j` from `indexDifference` to `n - 1`. The newly allowed index is `i = j - indexDifference`.
3. If `nums[i]` beats the current minimum or maximum, update `minIndex` or `maxIndex`.
4. If `nums[j] - nums[minIndex] >= valueDifference`, return `[minIndex, j]`.
5. If `nums[maxIndex] - nums[j] >= valueDifference`, return `[maxIndex, j]`.
6. After the loop, no pair works: return `[-1, -1]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [5, 1, 4, 1]`, `indexDifference = 2`, `valueDifference = 4`. At `j = 2` the prefix is just index 0, so both pointers are 0; `4 - 5` and `5 - 4` are below 4. At `j = 3`, `i = 1` holds `1`, so `minIndex = 1`; `nums[3] - nums[1] = 0`, but `nums[0] - nums[3] = 5 - 1 = 4` qualifies, giving `[0, 3]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass with constant work per index.
- Space: O(1): two indices.

## Pitfalls

- `i` may equal `j`: with `indexDifference = 0` and `valueDifference = 0`, `[0, 0]` is valid.
- When `indexDifference >= n` the loop never runs; the answer is `[-1, -1]`.
- Test both directions: `nums[j]` may be far above the minimum or far below the maximum.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `j` | right index of the pair being tried |
| `i` | index that just became far enough from `j` |
| `minIndex` | index of the smallest value in `nums[0..j - indexDifference]` |
| `maxIndex` | index of the largest value in that prefix |

narration.2: Index of the smallest value among the indices far enough to the left; index 0 is the first one allowed.
narration.3: Index of the largest value in that same prefix.
narration.4: Try each right index j that has at least one partner indexDifference places to its left.
narration.5: Index i has just come within reach: it is exactly indexDifference before j.
narration.6: Is the newly reachable value a new prefix minimum?
narration.7: Remember where the smallest value is.
narration.9: Is it a new prefix maximum?
narration.10: Remember where the largest value is.
narration.12: The smallest earlier value gives nums[j] its biggest gain; is the gap large enough?
narration.13: Yes: the prefix minimum and j form a valid pair.
narration.15: The largest earlier value gives the biggest drop; is that gap large enough?
narration.16: Yes: the prefix maximum and j form a valid pair.
narration.19: No right index found a partner, so no valid pair exists.
